correctness.rationale: For a generic central section, each polygon vertex corresponds bijectively to a crossing of one of the 30 icosahedron edges. Its endpoint sign is constant within each of the spherical chambers determined by six great circles. Every spherical chamber corner arises from one of the 30 oriented pair intersections; a full exact Z[sqrt(5)] test of all 64 sign masks and all 30 candidate crosses proves that there are precisely 20 triangular chambers with 12 crossings and 12 pentagonal chambers with 10 crossings. The six normals have no triple dependence. With theta=arccos(1/sqrt(5)), the standard Haar edge-separation identity yields expected crossings 30 theta/pi, and the two-point support then yields the probabilities. Girard gives independent total spherical area 20(3 theta-pi)+12(2 pi-5 theta)=4 pi. The included verifier checks exact signs without tolerances; the analytic argument extends from finitely many cells to all generic normals.

originality.rationale: The most relevant full-text article (De Loera et al., arXiv:2412.12419) discusses possible section vertex counts and a gap for the icosahedron, but not the random central Haar two-point law. Jeon (arXiv:2603.00017) analyzes one equatorial decagon rather than generic random sections. Kabluchko and Seidel (arXiv:2006.09492) cover regular simplex, cube, and crosspolytope sections, not the regular icosahedron. Frederick (2023) already describes the 20/12 spherical triangle-pentagon partition, and MathPages has already tabulated both spherical chamber area fractions; those components are explicitly prior work. These already determine the claimed probability once the chamber-section incidence types are known. The present claim pairs cell types with section types and supplies exact measure and mean. Searches for equivalent formulas and implications found no matching statement, subject to genuine residual overlap risk.
residual_risks: The 20-triangle/12-pentagon great-circle partition was already described in 2023, so the novelty is not that tessellation itself.
The new incidence labeling, in conjunction with older geometric facts, is elementary enough that an unindexed stereology or recreational-geometry account might implicitly give the probability law.
A semantic search and targeted full-text inspections do not certify global novelty.

The MathPages numerical area table reproduces nearly the entire probability arithmetic once one identifies the section types; the originality and value depend on the exact chamber-to-section incidence classification not having already appeared elsewhere.

value.rationale: The icosahedron is the first highly symmetric regular polytope beyond the simplex/cube/crosspolytope families, and its 2024 literature exhibits gaps in possible section vertex counts. The exact Haar law is a complete natural geometric-probability invariant: it classifies all generic normal directions, identifies their 10/12 section types, supplies exact probabilities and expectation, and relates edge crossing to a known spherical tessellation. It is a self-contained benchmark for random-polytope sections rather than a routine restatement of the known tessellation. Its scope is limited to regular centered icosahedron sections; that narrowness is explicit.
